sm: Todd Friel opens by arguing that sex was invented by God and is not dirty, and that it is sin that makes a mess of it. He says that if Jesus is in control of everything, intimacy is also about Christ, and that knowing this can help couples who have been frustrated. The rest of the part is an interview with Dr. John Crotz about Friel's book, Go Serve Your King. Friel explains the phrase came from an old Christian song asking what you would do for a king. He says many believers feel detached and purposeless because they miss the reality that God made the universe so his Son could redeem sinners. He contrasts his grace-based approach with John Mark Comer's spiritual disciplines and Rick Warren's purpose driven life, and begins to defend calling Jesus beautiful.

Friel says Jesus is the standard of all beauty, and that the Puritans were comfortable calling the King beautiful. He says bad evangelical teaching has made people shy away from that kind of language. Staring at Jesus as revealed in Scripture stirs the affections and moves truth from head to heart. Asked whether Jesus is Lord of the bedroom, Friel says intimacy is a good gift that includes pleasure, procreation and oneness, and that Ephesians 5 makes marriage a picture of the gospel. Because the gospel is sacrificial service, he says each spouse should be a servant rather than a taker or demander. He adds that trouble in the bedroom signals trouble elsewhere in the home, and that intimacy points to the greater joy of heaven.

Crotz asks about Christ's lordship over aging. Friel says people try to hide aging, but it is ordained by God and falls under Jesus' authority. He calls white hair a crown, a sign of wisdom and of getting closer to home. He says a facelift is not a sin unless it becomes an idol, but that believers need not follow the world's message that youth is everything. Crotz then notes that the book ends with practical means of growth and that there are no secrets to the Christian life. Friel says a Christian cannot become what God wants outside the local church. He calls church a school of character, says hearing your own pastor is better than watching a famous preacher online, and says gifts can only be used and received there.

Friel finishes his case for the local church, saying it lets you serve and be served and that elders will pursue you if you drift. Crotz closes the interview with James 1:22 about being doers of the word. Friel then reads from his book that pleasurable intimacy in a lifelong marriage is a faint reflection of the joy believers will have with God. He says it is an aperitif that whets the appetite for heaven, where there will be no sex but a greater, non-sexual closeness with God and everyone else. He draws applications: the gospel is about giving, sacrifice and setting aside rights, so intimacy should not be selfish. He also says purity teaching in the Josh Harris era stressed disease and danger instead of presenting sex as a wonderful gift meant for marriage.
